# Aṭṭhasaddajātaka (Ja 418)
**ID:** Ja 418
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Aṭṭhasaddajātaka* (Ja 418), translated as *The Eight Sounds*, is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka section of the Pali canon [Catalog; SuttaCentral]. Set while the Buddha was residing at Jetavana, the story was occasioned by a terrifying, indistinguishable sound heard at midnight by the king of Kosala [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The framing circumstance resembles that of the *Lohakumbhijātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. When the king anxiously inquires what the omen portends, the Buddha reassures him that no harm will occur, explaining that kings of old had heard identical sounds and initially prepared to perform a sacrifice of four animals of each kind upon the advice of brahmins; however, after listening to the counsel of wise men, they released the sacrificial beasts and had a drum beaten through the city to ban all slaughter [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The Buddha then recites the tale of the past beginning with the verse *Idam pure ninnam āhū ti* ("A pool so deep") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the past king is identified as Ānanda, the youth (*māṇava*) as Sāriputta, and the ascetic (*tāpasa*) as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].
SuttaCentral records four translations of the text in four languages [SuttaCentral]. No cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan are noted by SuttaCentral or found with significant scores by DharmaNexus [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus detects Pali-internal text reuse between this canonical Jātaka and the commentary in the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Atk S0513a3), comprising seven matching passages (686 matched characters), with the primary alignment spanning segments §1.1–1.6 [DharmaNexus]. The text and its commentary were edited in Roman characters by V. Fausböll in 1883 [Fausböll 1883].
